1320: Confidentiality is not absolute. There are situations in which not acting can be a greater risk.
1322: Risk to the person themselves (e.g. intense hopelessness, thoughts of self-harm, loss of control)
1323: Risk to others (e.g. aggressive or dysregulated behaviour)
1324: Serious situations in the workplace (e.g. harassment, violence, intense psychological distress)
1325: In these cases, it is important to
1326: not take on the responsibility alone
1327: seek appropriate support (line manager, HR, health services, etc.)
1328: wherever possible, tell the person what is going to be done
1330: “I’m worried about you and I think it’s important that we involve more support. Can I help with that?”
1332: The role of the person offering support is not to replace a professional, but to offer initial support and make it easier to access help.
1337: making it easier to access resources
1342: It is important to be clear that
1343: Supporting is not clinical intervention. Supporting is not solving the problem. Supporting is not taking responsibility for the other person’s wellbeing.

1356: recognise that it is not possible to help alone

1371: Distress does not always come from work. Sometimes a colleague is coping with a loss or a serious personal concern – and yet they are still there, present, trying to carry on. The way to offer support is essentially the same, but the context calls for even greater care and less urgency to “sort things out”.

1380: This guide organises the intervention in six steps, which help to structure the approach without making it rigid. You do not have to follow every step in a straight line.
1382: Quick guide: how to support a colleague
1383: You do not need to “get everything right”. Consistency matters more than perfection.
1384: Not every conversation moves forward; respecting the person’s pace is essential.
1385: Small gestures (being present, listening) can have a big impact.
1386: Helping a colleague does not require complex answers. It requires presence, structure and respect for the person’s pace.
1387: This guide is meant as support, not as a rigid rule.

1394: If the support involves the Occupational PhysicianGive an expected time window for observation. If the timeframe cannot be guaranteed, immediately activate an alternative (We Are Sonae helpline 800 100 025 – 24h, psychological support or an external resource).
1395: I noticed that something is not right with a colleague.
1396: Am I in a position to approach them now? If not: find another moment or involve someone who is available. If so: approach simply: “I wanted to know how you are.” “I noticed you seem more overwhelmed.”
1397: Does the person want to talk? If not: respect that. “If you want to talk later, I’m available.”
1398: What is most needed right now? Calm / stabilise: presence, calm tone, a pause. Organise / talk: listening, giving space, helping to clarify. Practical support: “Can I help with anything?”
1399: Is there a need for additional support? If so: “Would you like me to help you talk to someone?” “We can look together at what support makes sense.” Depending on the situation, refer them to the resources available. If not: stay available.
